title: Civil disobedience
hook: his essay argued that conscience comes before law (Resistance to Civil Government)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a night in jail: a shoe at the cobbler's, a locked cell, and huckleberries in the morning. What did you notice yourself going along with? Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

A rule says one thing. Something quieter says another. Most days the two agree, and nobody has to choose. But every so often they split, and a person has to decide which voice gets the final word. After his night in jail, Thoreau worked out his answer in public, in an essay called Resistance to Civil Government. It's often known now as Civil Disobedience. Today, the argument at its heart.
screen: `THE RULE SAYS ONE THING.` → `CONSCIENCE SAYS ANOTHER.` → `WHICH ONE WINS?`

segments.voice: First, what he isn't saying. The essay opens with a motto he says he heartily accepts, "That government is best which governs least." But a little further on, he's careful: he asks, he says, not for no government at once, but for a better government at once. This isn't a call to tear everything down. Second, the central question. Here it is in his words: "Must the citizen ever for a moment, or in the least degree, resign his conscience to the legislator? Why has every man a conscience, then?" If conscience can always be overruled by a vote, he asks, what is it for? Third, his answer. "I think that we should be men first, and subjects afterward. It is not desirable to cultivate a respect for the law, so much as for the right." Conscience first. Law matters, but it isn't the deepest thing. When a law requires you to do wrong to another person, he says, break the law. Fourth, how small it can start. He doesn't ask for an army. He asks each person to stop lending a hand to the wrong. "Let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine." A machine runs on many small cooperations. Withdraw yours, and the machine has a little less to run on. That's what the night in jail was: one person's friction, openly given, with the cost accepted. Not hidden. Not violent. Civil. That word matters as much as disobedience.
screen: `NOT NO GOVERNMENT. A BETTER ONE.` · `WHY HAS EVERY MAN A CONSCIENCE?` · `MEN FIRST, SUBJECTS AFTERWARD.` · then, large: `A COUNTER FRICTION TO STOP THE MACHINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow conscience in one small thing. Settle and breathe. Ask that quieter voice one question: is there something small I've been going along with that doesn't sit right? A joke at someone's expense. A shortcut at work. A purchase. A silence. Let one thing come. Then picture the smallest honest act of friction you could offer. Not a fight. Just declining, openly and calmly, to lend your hand to it. Hold that picture until it feels doable. The bell holds the time.
Civil disobedience. Thoreau's essay: when law and conscience split, put conscience first, openly and without violence. Today's word.
Your line: conscience first. Today, in one small place, do the right thing even if no rule asks it of you, and do it in the open. Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Thoreau's essay often take it as a case for putting conscience before law: refusing, openly and without violence, to cooperate with what one sees as wrong, and accepting the cost.
